newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Uganda military spending may hamper debt relief.
newsitem.headline: Uganda military spending may hamper debt relief.

text.p: The rise in Uganda's military spending is raising doubts about its economic reforms and delaying plans to make it the first beneficiary of international debt relief for the very poorest countries, diplomats said on Wednesday.
Germany and a number of other countries have questioned Uganda's military spending, using figures which show it has risen to 20 percent of the state budget from 13 percent six years ago.

They have linked the rise in military spending to civil wars in north and southwest Uganda, and alleged support by President Yoweri Museveni's government for rebels in Sudan and Zaire and for the government in Rwanda.
The diplomats were in Addis Ababa for a meeting of African financial officials and major lenders focusing on debt relief and financial sector reforms in Africa.

Uganda's government denies Sudanese and Zairean government accusations that it has sent troops into Sudan and eastern Zaire to fight alongside rebels. The government of Rwanda took power in 1994 following a rebel invasion from Uganda in 1990.

"Uganda stands tops in terms of the (economic reform) criteria. But Germany and others have questioned a rise in the military budget. Since Uganda is the first candidate, no one wants issues that may serve as precedent to be ignored," one senior diplomat said.

Last month the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank approved a debt relief plan for Uganda, making it the first candidate for the Debt Initiative for Heavily Indebted Countries (HIPC) which would ease debt owed to multilateral creditors.
The initiative could cut $385 million from Uganda's $3.4 billion international debt. About 70 percent of Uganda's external debt is owed to multilateral organisations.

But concerns among members of the boards of the IMF and World Bank mean Uganda cannot expect to benefit as early as it had hoped -- in September. Some countries want to review progress between April and November next year while others have suggested April 1999.

"We are not helping rebels in fighting Sudan or Zaire. We have our own wars in the north, with (Joseph) Kony's Lord's Resistance Army. How can we help others when we have failed to win that war for eight years," Ugandan Minister of State for Finance Basoga Nsandhu told Reuters.
Ugandan officials rejected the military spending figures in the hands of Western diplomats. Nsandhu said Uganda wanted them to visit Uganda "to avoid further expansion of rumours".
But he did not give real military spending figures.

In general, a country is required under the debt-relief initiative to establish a six-year record with IMF tutorship that shows strong economic reforms, although substantial flexibility is provided on a case-by-case basis.

The initiative was undertaken when it became clear that the repayment of old loans to lending agencies such as the World Bank and IMF were draining some of the poorest countries, making it impossible for them to get on their feet no matter what reform efforts they made.
Callisto Madavo, a World Bank Vice-President for Africa, said of Uganda's case: "There is nothing peculiar. A short delay is not a major loss to Uganda. We are being thorough."
